problems.stem: Which of the following is the most useful learning objective for guiding assessment design?
options: Given a captured packet trace and an intrusion-detection rulebook, the security analyst will identify all suspicious flows with at least 90% precision and recall.
Learners will appreciate the importance of cybersecurity.
Learners will be familiar with packet analysis.
problems.explanation: Audience (security analyst), behavior (identify suspicious flows), condition (given trace and rulebook), and degree (>=90% precision and recall) are all explicit. The others rely on unmeasurable verbs.

problems.stem: An objective uses the verb 'evaluate' but the planned assessment asks the learner only to recall a definition. What is the defect?
options: There is no defect; recall always supports evaluation.
The assessment does not match the cognitive level of the objective; it tests Remember while the objective claims Evaluate.
The objective should be lowered to Remember.
Bloom's taxonomy does not apply to assessment alignment.
problems.explanation: Constructive alignment requires the assessment to test the same cognitive level the objective claims. A recall item cannot validate an Evaluate objective.

problems.stem: An objective reads: 'The learner will analyze and evaluate a case study and design an intervention plan.' Why is this problematic?
options: It stacks three different performances at three different cognitive levels, hiding what success means and what to assess.
It uses Bloom verbs, which are not allowed in objectives.
problems.explanation: Stacked objectives obscure the assessment target. Split into three: one Analyze, one Evaluate, one Create.

problems.stem: What is the central commitment of constructive alignment?
options: All objectives must come from a textbook.
Objectives, assessment items, and practice activities must agree on what the learner is being asked to do, at the same cognitive level.
Only summative tests count as alignment evidence.
Activities should be harder than assessments.
problems.explanation: Constructive alignment (Biggs) is the principle that objectives, assessment, and activities must converge on the same performance.
